_schema: Payment processors for trades/contractors (Phase 2 category added 2026-05-28). Trade-agnostic; grouped by pricing_model. Rates are verified-as-of verified_date and change often; re-verify quarterly. affiliate_url stays 'TBD' until tracking is confirmed.

processors.name: Square
processors.tagline: Flat-rate payments, invoicing and POS with a no-monthly-fee plan
processors.pricing_summary: Flat-rate. Square Free ($0/mo): in-person 2.6% + 15¢, online and invoices 3.3% + 30¢, manually keyed or card on file 3.5% + 15¢. Square Plus ($49/mo per location): in-person 2.5% + 15¢, online and invoices 2.9% + 30¢. Square Premium ($149/mo per location): in-person 2.4% + 15¢, online and invoices 2.9% + 30¢. ACH bank transfer on invoices 1% ($1 minimum; $10 cap on Plus and Premium). Cards issued outside the US add 1.5%
processors.monthly_fee: $0 (Square Free); $49 or $149/mo per location (Square Plus or Premium)
processors.long_description:
Square is the payments and point-of-sale business of Block, Inc., which renamed itself from Square, Inc. to Block in 2021. Square's own timeline starts in 2009 with its original mobile card reader, and Block's SEC filings list its offices in Oakland, California. Square says more than four million sellers run on it. You sign up online, and the Square Free plan has no monthly fee.

For a trade business, the useful pieces are Square Invoices and in-person payments. Square Invoices covers estimates and contracts with e-signature, upfront deposits with a separate due date for the balance, recurring invoices and automatic payment reminders. In the field, Tap to Pay on iPhone and Android takes contactless cards with no reader; Square lists a free magstripe reader and a $59 contactless and chip reader. Square also sells payroll (from $35/mo plus $6 per person paid) and business banking, and QuickBooks Online can import Square transactions automatically.

On Square Free, in-person cards cost 2.6% + 15¢, online and invoice payments 3.3% + 30¢, and manually keyed or card-on-file payments 3.5% + 15¢. Square Plus ($49/mo per location) and Square Premium ($149/mo per location) lower the in-person rate to 2.5% + 15¢ and 2.4% + 15¢ and the online and invoice rate to 2.9% + 30¢. A Square community manager posted in November 2025 that the standard online processing fee would rise from 2.9% + 30¢ to 3.3% + 30¢ on January 13, 2026. ACH bank payments on invoices cost 1% with a $1 minimum, capped at $10 on Plus and Premium.

The trade-off: flat rates are simple but carry the same markup on every card, so a shop with high card volume or large tickets should compare its effective rate with interchange-plus or subscription processors and steer big invoices to ACH. Square's payment terms also let it defer payouts, delay transfers or hold a reserve during an investigation or when it sees chargeback risk, so a contractor who depends on one large payment should keep a cash buffer.
processors.how_it_works: You sign up online and can take payments in person (tap, dip or swipe with a Square reader, or Tap to Pay on iPhone and Android with no reader), online, through Square Invoices, or by keying in a card or charging a card on file. Each payment is charged a flat rate set by your plan: Square Free has no monthly fee, while Square Plus ($49/mo per location) and Square Premium ($149/mo per location) lower the rates. Square says payments taken before 5 PM PT arrive in your bank the next business day; instant and same-day transfers cost 1.95% per transfer. Invoices can collect cards or ACH bank payments, and payroll and banking sit in the same Square account.

pros_detail.title: Online sign-up, no contract
pros_detail.explanation: You sign up online, and Square's pricing page says there are no locked-in contracts and you can cancel or switch plans anytime. The Free plan has no monthly fee, so a solo contractor can start without a fixed cost.

pros_detail.title: Published flat rates
pros_detail.explanation: Every rate is on Square's fee page, so you know the cost of a payment before you take it: on the Free plan, 2.6% + 15¢ in person and 3.3% + 30¢ online or by invoice.

pros_detail.title: Invoicing that fits job work
pros_detail.explanation: Square Invoices includes estimates, contracts with e-signature, upfront deposits with a later due date for the balance, recurring invoices for maintenance plans and automatic reminders.

pros_detail.title: Low-cost ways to take cards on site
pros_detail.explanation: Tap to Pay on iPhone and Android needs no reader, Square lists the magstripe reader as free, and the contactless and chip reader is $59.

pros_detail.title: Adjacent tools in one account
pros_detail.explanation: Square Payroll (from $35/mo plus $6 per person paid) and Square Banking sit in the same account, and QuickBooks Online can import Square transactions automatically.

cons_detail.title: Flat-rate markup at volume
cons_detail.explanation: You pay the same percentage whatever a card's underlying cost, so at high card volume an interchange-plus or subscription processor can cost less. Work out your own effective rate before you commit.

cons_detail.title: Higher online rate on the Free plan
cons_detail.explanation: A Square community manager announced that the standard online processing fee rose from 2.9% + 30¢ to 3.3% + 30¢ on January 13, 2026. Square's fee page now lists 3.3% + 30¢ for online and invoice payments on the Free plan.

cons_detail.title: Payouts can be held
cons_detail.explanation: Square's payment terms let it defer payouts or restrict access to funds during an investigation, hold a reserve, and delay payouts when chargebacks are pending. A contractor who depends on one large payment is exposed if that happens.

cons_detail.title: Lower rates cost a monthly fee
cons_detail.explanation: The reduced rates require Square Plus at $49/mo or Square Premium at $149/mo, charged per location. At that point, compare the total cost with processors that price differently.

cons_detail.title: Percentage fees add up on big tickets
cons_detail.explanation: A $15,000 invoice paid by card online on the Free plan costs $495.30 at 3.3% + 30¢. The same invoice paid by ACH costs 1%, or $150 on Free and $10 on Plus or Premium because of the cap.

processors.best_for: Solo and small service businesses that want online sign-up, published flat rates, built-in invoicing and low-cost ways to take cards on site
processors.weaknesses: Flat-rate markup costs more at high card volume; Free-plan online and invoice rate is 3.3% + 30¢ since January 2026; payment terms allow payout holds and reserves; lower rates require a $49 or $149 monthly plan per location
processors.affiliate_payout_note: No confirmed affiliate program; we currently earn nothing from Square

faqs.q: What are Square's payment processing fees?
faqs.a: On Square Free: in person 2.6% + 15¢, online and invoices 3.3% + 30¢, and manually keyed or card on file 3.5% + 15¢. Square Plus ($49/mo per location) lowers these to 2.5% + 15¢ in person and 2.9% + 30¢ online; Square Premium ($149/mo per location) lowers in person to 2.4% + 15¢. ACH on invoices is 1% with a $1 minimum, capped at $10 on Plus and Premium, and cards issued outside the US add 1.5%.

faqs.q: Is Square a cheap option for a contractor?
faqs.a: It is simple and has no monthly fee on the Free plan, but a flat rate charges the same markup on every card. As your card volume or average ticket grows, compare your effective rate with interchange-plus or subscription processors, and consider the Plus or Premium plan only if the lower rates cover the monthly fee.

faqs.q: Can Square hold my funds?
faqs.a: Yes. Square's payment terms say it may defer payouts or restrict access to your proceeds during an investigation, hold a reserve that it can raise or lower at its discretion, and delay payouts while chargebacks are pending. If you take large or irregular payments, keep a cash buffer or a backup way to get paid.

faqs.q: Should a contractor use Square or the payments built into their field-service app?
faqs.a: If your field-service app offers its own card processing, that keeps payments in the same system as the job. Square makes sense if you want a standalone processor with invoicing, a POS and hardware, or if its rates beat your app's. Compare effective rates and where you want payments to reconcile.

faqs.q: Is Square good for big-ticket jobs?
faqs.a: Card fees get large on big invoices: a $15,000 invoice paid by card online on the Free plan costs $495.30 at 3.3% + 30¢. Square Invoices can also take ACH bank payments at 1% ($1 minimum), which Square caps at $10 on the Plus and Premium plans, so steering large invoices to ACH saves real money.

processors.name: Stripe
processors.tagline: Flat-rate online payments, cheap ACH and billing tools that other software builds on
processors.pricing_summary: Flat-rate, no setup or monthly fees. Online domestic cards 2.9% + 30¢ (manually entered cards +0.5%, international cards +1.5%, currency conversion +1%); in person with Stripe Terminal 2.7% + 5¢ (Tap to Pay adds 10¢ per authorization); ACH Direct Debit 0.8% capped at $5. Add-ons: Stripe Invoicing 0.4% per paid invoice (Starter) or 0.5% (Plus), Stripe Billing 0.7% of billing volume on pay-as-you-go, Instant Payouts 1.5% (50¢ minimum), $15 per dispute received
processors.headquartered: San Francisco, California and Dublin, Ireland
processors.long_description:
Stripe is a payments infrastructure company led by its cofounders, Patrick Collison (CEO) and John Collison (President). Stripe says it launched in 2010 and has dual headquarters in San Francisco and Dublin, and its 2025 annual letter says businesses on Stripe generated $1.9 trillion in payment volume that year. Like Square, it charges flat rates with no setup or monthly fees, and its products cover online payments, recurring billing and software that embeds payments.

Contractors can meet Stripe inside other software: Stripe's customer story on Jobber says the field-service app uses Stripe Connect, Terminal, Instant Payouts, Billing and Invoicing. Used directly, Stripe offers no-code Payment Links you can paste into a text or email or turn into a QR code, invoices sent from the Stripe Dashboard, Stripe Billing for recurring maintenance-plan charges, and a Stripe app built by Xero that lets customers pay Xero invoices by card.

Online domestic cards cost 2.9% + 30¢, with 0.5% more for manually entered cards and 1.5% more for international cards. In person, Stripe Terminal costs 2.7% + 5¢ per card, readers are $59 (Reader M2) or $299 (S700 and S710), and Tap to Pay on iPhone and Android adds 10¢ per authorization. ACH Direct Debit costs 0.8% capped at $5, which is where Stripe saves the most on large invoices: a $1,000 invoice costs $29.30 by online card and $5 by ACH, before any Invoicing fee.

The trade-off: Stripe gives you building blocks rather than a ready-made shop system, and add-on fees for Invoicing, Billing and Tap to Pay stack on top of the payment rate. Card fees are a flat percentage, so the savings on big jobs come from ACH, not cards. Stripe's services agreement also lets it hold a reserve and suspend an account it believes carries unacceptable or fraud risk.
processors.how_it_works: You can use Stripe through software that has it built in, such as a field-service app or website. You can also use it directly: create no-code Payment Links, send invoices from the Stripe Dashboard with Stripe Invoicing (0.4% per paid invoice on Starter, on top of payment fees), set up recurring charges with Stripe Billing (0.7% of billing volume on pay-as-you-go), and collect ACH Direct Debit at 0.8% capped at $5. For in-person payments, Stripe Terminal costs 2.7% + 5¢ per card, and Tap to Pay on a phone instead of a reader adds 10¢ per authorization. There are no setup or monthly fees, and Instant Payouts to your bank cost 1.5% of the payout (50¢ minimum).

pros_detail.title: Cheap ACH on large invoices
pros_detail.explanation: ACH Direct Debit costs 0.8% capped at $5, so a $1,000 invoice costs $5 by ACH versus $29.30 by online card at 2.9% + 30¢. The gap widens as invoices grow.

pros_detail.title: Recurring billing and invoicing
pros_detail.explanation: Stripe Billing handles recurring charges for maintenance plans at 0.7% of billing volume, and Stripe Invoicing sends invoices from the Dashboard at 0.4% per paid invoice; the 0.5% Plus plan adds quotes.

pros_detail.title: No-code ways to get paid
pros_detail.explanation: Payment Links need no code: you create a payment page in a few clicks and share it as a link or QR code, and invoices can be sent from the Stripe Dashboard.

pros_detail.title: No setup or monthly fees
pros_detail.explanation: Stripe says it charges no setup fees, monthly fees or closure fees on its standard pricing, so you pay only per transaction and for the add-ons you use.

pros_detail.title: Already inside other tools
pros_detail.explanation: Stripe's customer story says Jobber runs its payments on Stripe Connect and Terminal, and Xero offers its own Stripe app for card payments on Xero invoices.

cons_detail.title: Less turnkey for on-site card taking
cons_detail.explanation: Stripe positions Terminal around custom POS builds or its no-code option, with readers at $59-$299. A contractor who mostly takes cards on site may find a POS-first app simpler to run.

cons_detail.title: Add-on fees stack
cons_detail.explanation: Invoicing (0.4%-0.5% per paid invoice), Billing (0.7%), manual card entry (+0.5%) and Tap to Pay (+10¢) are charged on top of the base payment rate, so the real cost depends on which tools you use.

cons_detail.title: Flat card rates at volume
cons_detail.explanation: Online cards are 2.9% + 30¢ whatever the card's underlying cost, so at high card volume an interchange-plus or subscription processor can cost less. The big savings come from ACH.

cons_detail.title: Reserves and suspensions possible
cons_detail.explanation: Stripe's services agreement lets it hold a reserve against potential liabilities and suspend an account it believes raises fraud or presents unacceptable risk. Keep a cash buffer if you rely on large payments.

cons_detail.title: Dispute fee
cons_detail.explanation: Stripe charges $15 for each dispute you receive, which adds up for a business that sees frequent chargebacks on disputed jobs.

processors.best_for: Contractors who bill online or by invoice, want low-cost ACH on big-ticket and recurring billing, or already use software that runs on Stripe
processors.weaknesses: Less turnkey for on-site card taking than a POS-first app; add-on fees for Invoicing, Billing and Tap to Pay stack on the payment rate; flat card rates cost more at high volume (the savings come from ACH); services agreement allows reserves and suspensions
processors.affiliate_payout_note: No confirmed affiliate program; we currently earn nothing from Stripe

faqs.q: What are Stripe's fees?
faqs.a: Stripe has no setup or monthly fees. Online domestic cards cost 2.9% + 30¢, manually entered cards add 0.5%, international cards add 1.5%, and in-person cards through Stripe Terminal cost 2.7% + 5¢ (Tap to Pay adds 10¢ per authorization). ACH Direct Debit is 0.8% capped at $5. Stripe Invoicing adds 0.4% per paid invoice on Starter, Stripe Billing 0.7% on pay-as-you-go, Instant Payouts 1.5% (50¢ minimum), and each dispute costs $15.

faqs.q: Is Stripe good for contractors?
faqs.a: It fits contractors who bill online or by invoice, charge recurring maintenance plans, or want low-cost ACH on big jobs. Some field-service apps, Jobber among them, run their payments on Stripe. If you mostly take cards on site and want a ready-made POS, a POS-first processor may be simpler.

faqs.q: Stripe vs Square for a trades business?
faqs.a: Both are flat-rate. On their standard no-monthly-fee pricing, online cards are 2.9% + 30¢ on Stripe and 3.3% + 30¢ on Square Free, while in-person cards are 2.7% + 5¢ on Stripe and 2.6% + 15¢ on Square Free. For bank payments, Stripe ACH Direct Debit is 0.8% capped at $5, and Square's invoice ACH is 1% with a $1 minimum (capped at $10 on its paid plans). Square is more of a ready-made POS; Stripe is stronger for online billing and software integrations.

faqs.q: How much can ACH save on a big invoice?
faqs.a: On a $1,000 invoice, an online card costs $29.30 at 2.9% + 30¢ and ACH Direct Debit costs $5 because of the cap. On a $15,000 invoice, the card fee is $435.30 and ACH is still $5. Stripe Invoicing adds its per-invoice fee either way if you bill through it.

faqs.q: Do I need a developer to use Stripe?
faqs.a: Not for the basics. Payment Links need no code, invoices can be sent from the Stripe Dashboard, and Stripe offers a no-code option for Terminal. A custom checkout or POS build does take development work, or you can use Stripe through a tool that already integrates it.

processors.name: Helcim
processors.tagline: Interchange-plus card processing with a published margin and no monthly fee
processors.pricing_summary: Interchange-plus, no monthly fee. Helcim's margin on top of interchange starts at 0.40% + 8¢ in person and 0.50% + 25¢ keyed and online (up to $50K average monthly volume) and steps down automatically to 0.15% + 6¢ in person and 0.15% + 15¢ keyed and online above $1M. ACH 0.5% + 25¢, capped at $6 for transactions under $25,000
processors.long_description:
Helcim is a payment processor for small and mid-sized businesses, headquartered in Calgary, Alberta and led by founder and CEO Nic Beique. In August 2026 it announced a C$53 million Series C led by BDC's Growth Venture Fund, and it says it serves more than 22,000 active merchants across North America. It prices card payments on interchange-plus: you pay the card issuers' interchange and card-network fees at cost, plus Helcim's margin, which your monthly statement shows as its own line.

Helcim's margin starts at 0.40% + 8¢ for in-person cards and 0.50% + 25¢ for keyed and online cards, and it drops automatically as your average monthly volume over the last three months grows: 0.35% + 7¢ and 0.45% + 20¢ from $50K, 0.25% + 7¢ and 0.35% + 20¢ from $100K, 0.20% + 6¢ and 0.25% + 15¢ from $500K, and 0.15% + 6¢ and 0.15% + 15¢ above $1M. Helcim says it charges no monthly fee. ACH bank payments cost 0.5% + 25¢, capped at $6 for transactions under $25,000.

For a trade business, the toolset covers invoicing, recurring payments, a virtual terminal for phone payments, and a customer portal where clients pay open invoices and save cards or bank accounts. In the field you can use Helcim's card reader, its Smart Terminal or Tap to Pay on iPhone. Helcim connects to QuickBooks Online (Pay Now buttons on emailed invoices and Auto-Collect for recurring payments) and has its own app in the Xero App Store. Its Fee Saver feature passes card fees to customers as a surcharge or convenience fee where allowed; Helcim lists Connecticut, Colorado, Maine, Massachusetts and Oklahoma as restricted for in-person surcharges.

The trade-off: interchange-plus costs vary by card type, so statements take more reading than a single flat rate, and how much you save depends on your card mix and volume. Sign-up includes underwriting, which Helcim says usually takes a day or two, and Helcim may run periodic account reviews that can delay funds from your first batches.
processors.how_it_works: You apply online and go through underwriting, which Helcim says usually takes a day or two. Once approved, you take payments in person (Helcim card reader, Smart Terminal or Tap to Pay on iPhone), by phone through the virtual terminal, online, by invoice or on recurring schedules. Each card payment costs interchange and card-network fees at cost plus Helcim's margin, and your margin tier is set automatically from your average monthly volume over the last three months. Card deposits generally arrive 1-2 business days after your batch settles; eligible US merchants whose bank is on the RTP or FedNow networks can get next-business-day Faster Deposits at no extra cost on batches up to $25,000. ACH payments take 3-5 business days to arrive.

pros_detail.title: Published, itemized margin
pros_detail.explanation: Interchange and card-network fees pass through at cost, and Helcim's margin appears as its own line on your monthly statement, so you can check exactly what the processor keeps.

pros_detail.title: Automatic volume discounts
pros_detail.explanation: The margin steps down automatically across five tiers based on your three-month average volume, from 0.40% + 8¢ in person below $50K a month to 0.15% + 6¢ above $1M. No renegotiation is needed.

pros_detail.title: No monthly fee
pros_detail.explanation: Helcim says it charges no monthly fee, so a small or seasonal shop pays only per transaction and is not carrying a fixed cost through slow months.

pros_detail.title: Tools for invoiced and recurring work
pros_detail.explanation: Invoicing, recurring payments, a virtual terminal and a customer portal where clients pay invoices and save cards or bank accounts cover on-site, phone and maintenance-plan billing.

pros_detail.title: Low-cost ACH and fee pass-through
pros_detail.explanation: ACH costs 0.5% + 25¢, capped at $6 for transactions under $25,000, and Fee Saver can pass card fees to customers where surcharging or convenience fees are allowed.

cons_detail.title: Statements take more reading
cons_detail.explanation: Interchange-plus costs vary by card type, so your statement is less simple than a single flat rate. It suits an owner willing to track an effective rate rather than one headline number.

cons_detail.title: Underwriting at sign-up
cons_detail.explanation: Because it is a full merchant account, Helcim reviews your business before approval; it says underwriting usually takes a day or two and may ask about your processing needs and refund policies.

cons_detail.title: Account reviews can delay funds
cons_detail.explanation: Helcim's help center says it may run periodic account reviews and that a review can delay funds from your first transaction batches until it is complete.

cons_detail.title: Savings depend on your card mix
cons_detail.explanation: Rewards and business cards carry higher interchange, which passes straight through. The margin is low, but your total cost still depends on the cards your customers use.

cons_detail.title: ACH is slower than cards
cons_detail.explanation: ACH payments take 3-5 business days to arrive, versus 1-2 business days for card batches, which matters if you steer large invoices to ACH to save fees.

processors.best_for: Contractors processing steady card volume who want a published processing margin, automatic volume discounts and no monthly fee, and don't mind reading an interchange-plus statement
processors.weaknesses: Interchange-plus statements are more complex than a flat rate; underwriting at sign-up; periodic account reviews can delay early deposits; total cost depends on your customers' card mix
processors.affiliate_payout_note: No confirmed affiliate program; we currently earn nothing from Helcim

faqs.q: What is interchange-plus pricing?
faqs.a: Interchange-plus means you pay the card issuer's interchange and the card networks' fees at cost, which vary by card type, plus a fixed margin from the processor. Helcim's margin starts at 0.40% + 8¢ for in-person cards and 0.50% + 25¢ for keyed and online cards, and it shows as its own line on your monthly statement.

faqs.q: Is Helcim cheaper than Square?
faqs.a: It depends on your card mix and volume. Square Free charges a flat 2.6% + 15¢ in person, while Helcim charges interchange at cost plus 0.40% + 8¢, falling automatically as your volume grows. Pull a recent statement, look at your interchange costs and compare both on your own numbers.

faqs.q: Does Helcim have monthly fees or contracts?
faqs.a: Helcim says it charges no monthly fee; you pay per transaction. Its help center explains how to close an account yourself and does not mention a cancellation fee, but read your merchant agreement before you sign.

faqs.q: Helcim vs a subscription processor: which is cheaper?
faqs.a: A subscription processor charges a fixed monthly fee in exchange for a smaller markup on each payment, so it only pays off once your volume is high enough to cover the fee. Helcim has no monthly fee and lowers its margin automatically with volume. Compare both on your actual monthly volume and average ticket.

faqs.q: Are there downsides to Helcim?
faqs.a: Interchange-plus statements take more reading than a flat rate, and your total cost depends on the cards your customers use. Sign-up includes underwriting, and Helcim may run periodic account reviews that can delay funds from your first batches. ACH is cheap but takes 3-5 business days to arrive.

processors.name: Stax
processors.tagline: Subscription pricing: a monthly fee instead of a percentage markup on card payments
processors.pricing_summary: Subscription pricing. Stax's documentation says plans start at $99/month, with interchange passed through at cost and no percentage markup. Your plan and any per-transaction, ACH or hardware fees are quoted, so get the full fee schedule in writing
processors.long_description:
Stax Payments, formerly Fattmerchant, is a payment processor based in Orlando, Florida. Its BBB profile lists the former name, and The Business Journals reported the name change in April 2021. Stax sells subscription pricing: a monthly fee in place of a percentage markup on each card payment. In October 2025 it announced the launch of Stax Processing, which it described as completing its move to a full-stack, end-to-end payments processor.

Stax's documentation says its subscription pricing starts at $99 per month and that interchange is passed through without markup, so whether a sale is $50 or $5,000 you pay the processing cost with no percentage added. That is the appeal for a busy shop doing large tickets: the markup does not grow with the invoice. Your exact plan and any per-transaction, ACH or hardware fees come in a quote.

For a trade business, Stax's documentation covers invoices sent by email or text message, scheduled invoices for recurring or one-time billing, stored card and bank (ACH) payment methods for repeat customers, and WiFi card terminals. Stax also supports surcharging on credit cards, capped at 3%, and says Connecticut, Massachusetts and Puerto Rico prohibit it. New accounts go through underwriting; Stax says most applications get a first review within about 36-48 hours.

The trade-off: the monthly fee is a fixed cost whatever you process, so the model only pays off once your card volume is high enough, and slow seasons still carry the full fee. At $5,000 a month in card volume, a $99 fee adds about 2% on top of interchange. Stax's risk documentation also names account reserves and terminations as consequences of chargeback risk, so read the reserve terms and the full fee schedule before you sign.
processors.how_it_works: You apply and go through underwriting, which Stax says usually starts within about 36-48 hours. Stax then charges a monthly subscription (from $99, per its documentation) and passes interchange through at cost without a percentage markup; ask for any per-transaction and other fees in your quote. You take payments on Stax WiFi terminals, by invoices sent by email or text, on scheduled invoices for recurring billing, and with stored cards or bank accounts (ACH) for repeat customers. Because the markup is not a percentage, the model favors businesses with high card volume and large average tickets.

pros_detail.title: No percentage markup
pros_detail.explanation: Stax passes interchange through at cost and charges a subscription instead of a percentage on top, so a $5,000 invoice does not carry a bigger markup than a $50 one.

pros_detail.title: Fixed cost that favors volume
pros_detail.explanation: The subscription starts at $99/month. The more card volume you run through it, the smaller that fee becomes as a share of each dollar processed.

pros_detail.title: Invoicing and recurring billing
pros_detail.explanation: Invoices can go out by email or text, and scheduled invoices handle recurring maintenance-plan billing or one-time future charges.

pros_detail.title: Cards and bank accounts on file
pros_detail.explanation: Stax stores both card and bank (ACH) payment methods for customers, which helps with repeat work and large invoices paid by bank transfer.

pros_detail.title: Surcharging support
pros_detail.explanation: Stax can add a surcharge of up to 3% on credit cards where it is allowed, and says it guides merchants through setup to stay compliant. Debit cards cannot be surcharged.

cons_detail.title: Only pays off at sufficient volume
cons_detail.explanation: At $5,000 a month in card volume, a $99 fee adds about 2% on top of interchange. At lower volume, compare the total with a processor that has no monthly fee.

cons_detail.title: Fixed fee through slow months
cons_detail.explanation: The subscription is charged every month regardless of volume, which is harder on seasonal trades with long slow periods.

cons_detail.title: Full fee schedule is quoted
cons_detail.explanation: Stax's documentation publishes only the $99 starting price. Per-transaction, ACH, hardware and any other fees come in a quote, so get every fee in writing before you sign.

cons_detail.title: Underwriting and reserves
cons_detail.explanation: Accounts are underwritten before approval, and Stax's risk documentation names account reserves and terminations as consequences of chargeback risk. Read the reserve terms in your agreement.

cons_detail.title: Surcharging is not allowed everywhere
cons_detail.explanation: Stax says Connecticut, Massachusetts and Puerto Rico prohibit surcharging, so a shop there cannot use it to offset card costs.

processors.best_for: High-volume, higher-ticket contractors who process enough to cover a monthly subscription and want to avoid a percentage markup on card payments
processors.weaknesses: Monthly fee is dead weight below break-even volume; fixed cost through slow seasons; only the $99 starting price is published, so the rest of the fee schedule must be quoted; underwriting and possible reserves
processors.affiliate_payout_note: No confirmed affiliate program; we currently earn nothing from Stax

faqs.q: How does Stax subscription pricing work?
faqs.a: You pay a monthly subscription, which Stax's documentation says starts at $99, and interchange is passed through at cost with no percentage markup. Your exact plan and any per-transaction, ACH or hardware fees are quoted. The model saves money when your volume is high enough that the fixed fee costs less than a percentage markup would.

faqs.q: Is Stax cheaper than Square or Helcim?
faqs.a: Only at sufficient volume. Square Free charges a flat 2.6% + 15¢ in person with no monthly fee, and Helcim charges interchange plus 0.40% + 8¢ with no monthly fee. Stax replaces the percentage markup with a monthly fee from $99, so run your real monthly volume and average ticket through all three before switching.

faqs.q: What should I check before signing with Stax?
faqs.a: Ask for the complete fee schedule in writing: the monthly plan price for your volume, any per-transaction fees, ACH fees, hardware costs, contract length and any early termination fee. Also read the reserve terms, since Stax's risk documentation names reserves as a way it manages chargeback risk.

faqs.q: Who should use Stax?
faqs.a: High-volume, higher-ticket contractors, such as busy multi-crew operations with many large invoices, who process enough to cover the monthly subscription. Solo operators and lower-volume shops should compare the total with a processor that has no monthly fee.

faqs.q: Is the monthly fee a problem for seasonal trades?
faqs.a: It can be. The subscription is charged every month whatever you process, so a seasonal business pays it through slow months, which eats into the savings. Compare a full year of your real volume, not just a busy month.

processors.name: QuickBooks Payments / GoPayment
processors.tagline: Card, ACH and wallet payments that auto-match to your QuickBooks invoices
processors.pricing_summary: Pay-as-you-go with no monthly fee; rates are flat percentages. In person 2.5%; invoiced and online cards and digital wallets (Apple Pay, PayPal, Venmo) 2.99%; keyed-in cards 3.5%; Affirm buy now, pay later 2.99%; ACH bank payments 1% ($1 minimum). Instant deposits 1.75%. Optional payment dispute protection from 0.99% (up to $10,000 per dispute and $25,000 a year). Businesses processing over $2,500/mo can call Intuit about a volume discount of up to 25%. Rates as of 09/18/2026
processors.long_description:
QuickBooks Payments is Intuit's payment service for QuickBooks users. Customers can pay emailed invoices by card, ACH bank transfer, Apple Pay, PayPal, Venmo or Affirm's buy now, pay later, and Intuit says payments are auto-matched to invoices in QuickBooks Online, so your books update without double entry. GoPayment is the mobile app for taking cards in the field with a $49 QuickBooks card reader or Tap to Pay on iPhone, and QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise users get Desktop Payments inside Desktop.

Pricing is pay-as-you-go with no monthly fee: 2.5% in person, 2.99% for invoiced and online cards and digital wallets, 3.5% for keyed-in cards, 2.99% for Affirm, and 1% for ACH with a $1 minimum. Intuit's rate page (rates as of 09/18/2026) lists no cap on the ACH fee. Deposits arrive the next day as standard, or instantly for 1.75%. Optional dispute protection starts at 0.99% and covers up to $10,000 per dispute and $25,000 a year, and businesses processing more than $2,500 a month can call Intuit about a volume discount of up to 25%.

Intuit may hold payments for review. Its help center says new users' first few payments can take longer, that it may ask for the original invoice and up to six months of bank statements, and that it completes a review within 2 business days. On a large install payment, even a short hold can delay cash you were counting on.

The trade-off: the auto-matching only pays off if your books are in QuickBooks. GoPayment works without a QuickBooks subscription, but Intuit recommends one to keep payments and books in sync. Keyed cards at 3.5% and invoiced cards at 2.99% add up on office and phone payments, and because ACH is 1% with no listed cap, a $15,000 invoice paid by ACH still costs $150.
processors.how_it_works: Add QuickBooks Payments to your QuickBooks account. Customers pay emailed invoices online by card, ACH, Apple Pay, PayPal, Venmo or Affirm, or your techs take cards in person with the GoPayment app and a $49 card reader or Tap to Pay on iPhone. Payments are auto-matched to invoices in QuickBooks Online, and you can schedule recurring payments. Deposits are next day as standard or instant for 1.75%, and eligible payments into QuickBooks Checking deposit without a fee. There is no monthly fee and Intuit's rate page shows no monthly plan; businesses processing over $2,500 a month can call about a discount.

pros_detail.explanation: Intuit says payments are auto-matched to their invoices in QuickBooks Online, which removes double entry for any contractor whose books are already there.

pros_detail.explanation: Techs can take contactless cards on an iPhone with the QuickBooks or GoPayment app and no card reader to buy or carry.

pros_detail.explanation: Customers can pay an emailed invoice by card, ACH, Apple Pay, PayPal, Venmo or Affirm's buy now, pay later, which helps on large jobs where a customer wants to spread the cost.

pros_detail.explanation: ACH costs 1% with a $1 minimum, so a $5,000 invoice costs $50 by ACH versus $149.50 by card at 2.99%.

pros_detail.explanation: There is no monthly fee, deposits are next day as standard, and instant deposits are available for 1.75% when cash is tight.

cons_detail.explanation: Intuit's help center says it may put payments on hold, may ask for the original invoice and bank statements, and completes reviews within 2 business days. A hold on a big install payment can still disrupt payroll or supplier payments.

cons_detail.explanation: The reconciliation advantage only exists if QuickBooks is your accounting system; GoPayment works without a subscription, but Intuit recommends one to keep books in sync.

cons_detail.title: Keyed and invoiced card rates
cons_detail.explanation: Keyed-in cards cost 3.5% and invoiced or online cards 2.99%, higher than the 2.5% in-person rate, which adds up on phone and office payments.

cons_detail.title: ACH fee has no listed cap
cons_detail.explanation: ACH is 1% with no cap on Intuit's rate page, so a $15,000 invoice costs $150. Stripe caps its ACH Direct Debit fee at $5, and Square caps invoice ACH at $10 on its paid plans.

cons_detail.title: Tap to Pay is iPhone-only
cons_detail.explanation: Intuit says Android users need a QuickBooks card reader, so no-hardware acceptance is limited to iPhone.

processors.best_for: Contractors who already run their books in QuickBooks and want invoice payments that auto-match, with a cash buffer in case a large payment is held for review
processors.weaknesses: Payments can be held for review; value tied to using QuickBooks; keyed (3.5%) and invoiced (2.99%) card rates above the in-person rate; ACH fee has no listed cap; Tap to Pay limited to iPhone

faqs.a: Partly. Intuit says GoPayment does not require a QuickBooks subscription but recommends one to keep payments and books in sync. The main reason to choose QuickBooks Payments is that payments auto-match to invoices in QuickBooks Online; without QuickBooks as your books, you lose that and should compare it on rates alone.

faqs.q: Why might QuickBooks Payments hold my money?
faqs.a: Intuit's help center says it may put payments on hold to protect everyone in the payment process, and that new users' first few payments can take longer. During a review it may ask for the original invoice and up to six months of bank statements, and it says it completes reviews within 2 business days. faqs.q: Can field techs take cards with QuickBooks Payments?
faqs.a: Yes. The GoPayment app takes tap, dip or swipe payments with a $49 QuickBooks card reader, and Tap to Pay on iPhone takes contactless cards with no reader. Payments sync to QuickBooks. Intuit says Android users need the card reader.

processors.name: PayPal Point of Sale (formerly Zettle)
processors.tagline: No-monthly-fee card acceptance with Tap to Pay, invoicing and PayPal and Venmo payments
processors.pricing_summary: Point of sale: card-present and QR code 2.29% + $0.09; manual card entry 3.49% + $0.09. Invoices and online checkout: cards 2.99% + $0.49; PayPal or Venmo 3.49% + $0.49; Pay Later 4.99% + $0.49; ACH bank payment on invoices 1% capped at $10. No monthly or setup fee for PayPal Point of Sale, and sending invoices is free. Card reader $29 for a new business user's first reader, $79 each after; PayPal Terminal $199 ($239 with barcode scanner). Dispute fees $15 standard, $30 high volume. Instant transfer to a bank costs 1.5% (minimum fee applies). Optional paid services such as Payments Pro ($30/mo) are listed on PayPal's fee page.
processors.long_description:
PayPal lets a trade business take cards with no monthly fee. Its point-of-sale app, now called PayPal Point of Sale (formerly PayPal Zettle), works with Tap to Pay on a compatible phone, a PayPal card reader ($29 for a new business user's first reader, $79 after) or the $199 PayPal Terminal. PayPal says there are no monthly fees, startup fees or long-term commitments: you pay 2.29% + $0.09 for card-present and QR code payments and 3.49% + $0.09 for manually entered cards.

For billing after the job, PayPal Invoicing is free to send. When the customer pays, cards cost 2.99% + $0.49, PayPal or Venmo 3.49% + $0.49, and an ACH bank payment 1% capped at $10, so a large invoice paid by bank costs far less to collect than one paid by card. PayPal supports recurring invoices and automatic reminders, and its POS page lists integrations with QuickBooks, Xero and Shopify, plus inventory with low-stock alerts and sales reporting.

Payments land in your PayPal balance, which PayPal says gives access to money in minutes, and you can move the money to your bank. An instant transfer to a bank costs 1.5% of the amount, with a minimum fee. PayPal was founded in 1998 and is based in San Jose, California.

The trade-off: holds. PayPal's own help pages say it may hold payments, usually for up to 21 days, for new sellers, for sellers who have not sold in a while, and when a selling pattern changes, such as an unexpected surge in sales, which is what one big job can look like. It can also place reserves on an account. Manual card entry and card payments on invoices cost more than tapped cards, and dispute fees apply. Keep a separate business bank account and move money out regularly.
processors.how_it_works: Open a PayPal Business account, download the PayPal Point of Sale app, and take payments with Tap to Pay (iPhone XS or later, or Android 8.0 or later with NFC and Google Play Services), a PayPal card reader, or the PayPal Terminal. Customers can also pay by PayPal or Venmo QR code. For after-the-job billing, create and send invoices from your PayPal account; customers pay by card, PayPal, Venmo, Pay Later or ACH bank payment. Money arrives in your PayPal balance, subject to PayPal's transaction review and holds, and can then be transferred to your bank, or instantly for a 1.5% fee.

processors.weaknesses: Payment holds, usually up to 21 days, for new sellers or unusual sales patterns; higher manual-entry and online card rates; PayPal and Venmo invoice payments cost 3.49% + $0.49; dispute fees; 1.5% fee for instant transfers

faqs.a: PayPal is a long-established payments company, founded in 1998 and based in San Jose, California. faqs.q: Does PayPal integrate with my accounting or FSM software?
faqs.a: PayPal's POS page lists integrations with QuickBooks, Xero and Shopify, and PayPal says invoices can be automated with accounting software such as QuickBooks or Xero. If you run field-service software, check with that vendor whether it supports PayPal payments before relying on it.

processors.long_description:
Clover is Fiserv's point-of-sale system for small businesses. Fiserv describes it as an all-in-one system for taking payments "in your location, online and on the go", with point of sale, payments acceptance, online ordering, customer loyalty tools and an app marketplace. Fiserv says Clover handles more than $337 billion in annualized processing volume.

The hardware line includes the Station Solo and Station Duo counter systems, the Mini and Compact, the handheld Flex and Flex Pocket (both with 4G/LTE, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth), and Clover Go, a reader that pairs with an iPhone or Android phone and accepts chip and contactless payments, including Tap to Pay on iPhone. For a trade business that also runs a counter or showroom, one Clover account can cover both the counter and the field.

Pricing combines a monthly software plan, hardware and per-transaction processing fees. Clover is sold on its own website and through resellers, and offers can differ. We could not confirm Clover's current published prices for this update, so this listing no longer quotes plan, hardware or processing prices.

The trade-off: what you pay and how long you are committed depend on the deal you sign. Before committing, get the software plan, hardware price or rental terms, processing rates, contract length, any early-termination fee, and whether the hardware can be used with another processor if you leave, all in writing.
processors.how_it_works: Choose a Clover software plan and hardware, either on Clover's website or through a reseller, and a merchant processing account is set up for you. Take payments at the counter on a Station, Mini or Compact, in the field on a Flex or Flex Pocket handheld or a Clover Go reader paired with your phone, and online. Extend the system with apps from the Clover App Market. Because offers differ between sellers, compare written quotes before signing.

processors.name: Authorize.Net
processors.tagline: A no-contract payment gateway with an optional built-in merchant account, invoicing and recurring billing
processors.pricing_summary: Every plan: $25/mo gateway fee, $0 setup, no contract and no early-termination fee. All-in-One (merchant account included, subject to eligibility): 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction. Gateway Only (for businesses that already have a merchant account): $0.10 per transaction plus a $0.10 daily batch fee, on top of your processor's own fees. Gateway + eCheck adds eCheck payments at 0.75% per transaction, with a $10 monthly eCheck minimum, a $25 fee per eCheck chargeback and a $3 fee per returned eCheck (US businesses only). Account Updater costs $0.25 per update.
processors.headquartered: United States (a wholly owned subsidiary of Visa)
processors.long_description:
Authorize.Net is a payment gateway: the layer that connects your website, invoices, virtual terminal or mobile app to the card networks and your merchant account, with fraud screening, recurring billing and stored customer payment details. It has operated since 1996, is a wholly owned subsidiary of Visa, and says more than 430,000 merchants use it.

There are two main ways to use it. The All-in-One plan includes a merchant account at 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction plus the $25 monthly gateway fee. The Gateway Only plan keeps the merchant account you already have with a bank or payment provider and adds $0.10 per transaction and a $0.10 daily batch fee on top of your processor's rates. Every plan has no setup fee, no contract and no early-termination fee, and eCheck payments can be added at 0.75% per transaction for US businesses.

For trade work, Authorize.Net offers a Virtual Terminal for phone payments, digital invoices sent by email, monthly recurring or installment billing for service agreements, and a free mobile app with Tap to Pay on NFC phones or a card reader. It says its shopping cart plugins connect to Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, Magento and more than 170 other platforms, and its Advanced Fraud Detection Suite shows a $0 fee on the pricing page.

The trade-off: the $25 monthly fee applies even in a slow month, and on Gateway Only it sits on top of your processor's own fees. Chip-card reading in the mobile app works only on certain processor platforms (First Data Nashville and TSYS), and extras such as Account Updater ($0.25 per update) and eCheck minimums add cost. Confirm that your field-service or accounting software supports Authorize.Net before you sign up.
processors.how_it_works: Sign up for the All-in-One plan (gateway plus a merchant account) or, if you already have a merchant account, the Gateway Only plan. Then take payments through the Virtual Terminal, emailed digital invoices, recurring billing, a website or shopping cart plugin, or the free Authorize.net mobile app with Tap to Pay or a card reader. Authorize.Net routes each transaction to the card networks, screens it for fraud and can store customer payment details for repeat billing. All-in-One deposits card funds into your business bank account; Gateway Only customers are paid by their existing processor.

processors.headquartered: United States (BBB lists San Francisco, California and Montclair, New Jersey addresses)
processors.long_description:
Dharma Merchant Services is a US card processor that prices on an interchange-plus basis: you pay the interchange cost set by the card networks plus Dharma's markup, so the processor's own charge is shown separately. Dharma publishes rate pages for retail and small businesses, e-commerce and online sellers, and B2B processing, along with worked interchange-plus pricing examples.

BBB's San Francisco profile lists a business start date of March 1, 2007, names Jeffrey Marcous as CEO and lists seven employees; a second BBB profile gives a Montclair, New Jersey address. Neither profile shows complaints closed in the last three years.

Interchange-plus pricing can work out cheaper than a single flat percentage for a business with steady card volume when the markup is small, but the effective rate changes with the mix of cards your customers use, and any monthly fee weighs more when volume is low.

faqs.q: Is Dharma cheaper than a flat-rate processor?
faqs.a: It depends on your volume and card mix. Dharma uses interchange-plus pricing, where you pay the card networks' interchange cost plus a markup, while a flat-rate processor such as Square or Stripe charges a published percentage plus a fixed fee per transaction. Interchange-plus can work out cheaper with steady volume, but any monthly fee weighs more at low volume. Get Dharma's current fee schedule and compare it with a recent statement from your current processor.

processors.long_description:
pmtbox is the new name of National Processing, the Orem, Utah card processor. Its help center says the name changed on November 1, 2025, that the company was not acquired, and that Wayne Hamilton, who founded National Processing, is CEO and leads the same team; existing merchants keep the same rates, account terms, phone number and support team. pmtbox's site gives the company's name as Payment Box, Inc., a registered ISO/MSP of Commercial Bank of California and Chesapeake Bank. The old nationalprocessing.com domain no longer resolves.

The business has also repositioned. In April 2026 Payment Box, Inc. announced a $15 million seed round led by Tandem Ventures, described pmtbox as a platform that brings payments, risk and transaction data together, and said it serves roughly 1,300 customers. pmtbox.com says it handles payments, fraud and chargebacks for e-commerce brands under one fee, guarantees every transaction it approves, screens for fraud with machine learning, and offers one API across online, mobile and in-store payments.

For trade businesses, the help center still covers in-person and mobile payments, with guides for Dejavoo, Verifone and PAX terminals and the SwipeSimple mobile app, and its integrations list includes QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop, Xero and FreshBooks. BBB's profile for National Processing, LLC lists a business start date of October 1, 2007 and says its information is being updated, with no report available.

The trade-off: pmtbox publishes no rate card, plans or contract terms, so you cannot compare costs without a sales quote. Our earlier review raised concerns about fees and equipment-lease terms under the National Processing name that we could not re-verify, so get the full fee schedule, contract term, any early-termination fee and any PCI non-compliance fee in writing before signing.
processors.how_it_works: Fill in the contact-sales form on pmtbox.com, which asks for your estimated annual sales, and a pmtbox sales representative follows up with pricing and the steps to open a merchant account. pmtbox says it handles processing, fraud screening and chargebacks under one fee and covers fraud on transactions it approves. Its help center has setup guides for countertop terminals and the SwipeSimple mobile app. Existing National Processing merchants were told their rates, account terms, phone number and support team stay the same.

faqs.q: Is National Processing now pmtbox?
faqs.a: Yes. National Processing started using the pmtbox name on November 1, 2025. Its help center says the company was not acquired, that founder Wayne Hamilton is CEO and leads the same team, and that existing merchants keep the same rates, account terms, phone number and support team. The company behind it is Payment Box, Inc. of Orem, Utah, and the old nationalprocessing.com domain no longer resolves.

faqs.a: pmtbox publishes no rate card. Its help center says a sales representative sends pricing after you complete the contact-sales form. pmtbox says it handles payments, fraud and chargebacks under one fee, so get the complete fee schedule, contract term, any early-termination fee and any PCI non-compliance fee in writing before signing.

faqs.q: What happened to the warning on this listing?
faqs.a: Our earlier review of National Processing flagged fees that surfaced despite 'lowest fee' marketing and leased equipment tied to a multi-year term. We could not re-verify those terms: the old site is gone, pmtbox publishes no terms, and BBB says its information on National Processing, LLC is being updated with no report available. We removed the warning rather than repeat claims we cannot source today.

faqs.q: Is this the same as "National Payment Processing"?
faqs.a: Not necessarily: other payment companies use similar names. pmtbox's site gives its corporate name as Payment Box, Inc. and its address as 898 N 1200 W, Orem, Utah, and BBB lists National Processing, LLC at the same address. Confirm those details before you sign.
